content: Zika virus infection is caused by the Zika virus, which is an enveloped, single-stranded, positive-sense RNA virus. This virus belongs to the Flavivirus genus and is primarily transmitted to humans through mosquito vectors. The Zika virus, also referred to as ZIKV, is an enveloped, icosahedral virus with a single-stranded, positive-sense RNA genome. It is closely related to the Spondweni virus and is one of the two viruses in the Spondweni virus clade. The genome of the Zika virus is composed of 10,794 nucleotides, encoding 3,419 amino acids. It is a member of the Flaviviridae family and the Flavivirus genus. There are two distinct lineages of the Zika virus: the African lineage and the Asian lineage. The primary mode of Zika virus transmission to humans is through infected mosquitoes. The Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquito species are recognized as the main vectors for Zika virus transmission. These mosquitoes are known for their ability to thrive in tropical and subtropical regions. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) provides detailed information on the life cycle of Aedes aegypti mosquitoes. Zika virus can also be transmitted from human to human through two primary routes: mother-to-child transmission and sexual transmission. Mother-to-child transmission: A pregnant woman infected with the Zika virus can pass the virus to her fetus during pregnancy or around the time of delivery. The presence of Zika virus in amniotic fluid suggests that the virus can cross the placental barrier, making vertical transmission possible. Despite this, there are no reported cases of Zika virus transmission through breastfeeding. Given the nutritional benefits of breast milk, mothers are encouraged to breastfeed their infants even in areas where Zika virus is endemic. Sexual transmission: Zika virus can be transmitted sexually between humans, even if the infected individual is asymptomatic. The virus has been found to persist in semen longer than in other bodily fluids, such as vaginal fluids, urine, or blood. Zika virus can also be transmitted through blood transfusion. While no cases have been reported in the United States, there have been documented cases in Brazil, which are currently under investigation. In response, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued revised guidelines on August 26, 2016, recommending universal testing of donated whole blood and blood components for Zika virus in the United States and its territories. There has been one reported case of laboratory-acquired Zika virus infection in the United States. Following a mosquito bite, the incubation period for Zika virus in humans is approximately 3 to 12 days. The virus initially replicates in dendritic cells near the site of inoculation before spreading to lymph nodes and eventually the bloodstream. Zika virus can be inactivated by potassium permanganate, ether, and temperatures above 60°C, but it is not effectively neutralized by 10% ethanol. Detection of Zika virus is primarily achieved through the isolation of viral RNA from blood serum using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) in acutely ill patients. The CDC has also developed an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) to detect IgM antibodies against ZIKV. The viremia associated with Zika virus is short-lived, with the virus detectable in serum for 3 to 5 days following symptom onset. However, Zika virus can be detected in urine for up to 10 days after symptom onset.
